issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home' implies an interpersonal/home-intrusion threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items, which center on contamination/body danger and intrusive sensory reliving.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' is not impossible after chemical exposure, but here it reads as preparation for assault/entrapment rather than avoidance of fumes, contamination, or bodily symptoms; it is weakly aligned with the rest of the profile and the trauma context.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items focus strongly on social/cultural disconnection and not belonging, which is difficult to reconcile as the central appraisal pattern for a 60-year-old male whose trauma was toxic chemical exposure. These appraisals are not impossible, but alongside the rest of the profile they are poorly connected to the main symptom pattern of somatic threat, false alarms, and sensory reliving. A clinician would question why chemically exposure-related PTSD is expressed mainly as community/cultural alienation rather than danger, contamination, mistrust of body, or permanent harm beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the profile is dominated by body-based threat and intrusive sensory memory, but the maladaptive strategy item 'Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others' is not well supported because the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from all other nodes. Reminder-based avoidance centered on external prompts by others implies a trigger-driven maintenance pattern that is not reflected in the formulation or elsewhere in the self-report.

vignette:
Bao, a meticulous hotel manager of 60, had always taken pride in the seamless operation of his establishment. That was before the incident eight months ago. During a routine inspection of the chemical storeroom, a newly delivered drum of industrial cleaner, improperly sealed, had been slowly leaking a clear, odorless vapor. He walked into the enclosed space and the first thing he registered was a sharp, metallic taste that coated his tongue, followed by a wave of dizziness. He remembers the feeling of his lungs refusing to draw in air and the sight of the concrete floor rushing up to meet him before everything went dark.

The memory of that moment now operates on its own schedule. It forces its way into his mind without warning, often at work when he passes the laundry facilities or a housekeeping cart. When the memory arrives, it is not a simple recollection; he feels himself back in that storeroom, choking on the same acrid, metallic taste. This sudden, vivid reliving of the event triggers an immediate, powerful sense of danger. His heart begins to pound, and his entire body clenches as if bracing for another collapse. This intense physiological alarm sends him into a flurry of activity; he begins scanning his surroundings, checking air vents, and looking for any sign of a spill or leak. The memory serves as a constant, visceral reminder of his vulnerability, cementing a profound belief that he is utterly helpless to stop bad things from happening to him.

This deeply ingrained sense of helplessness now governs his existence. The belief that his body is unreliable and that he is fundamentally unsafe keeps him in a perpetual state of high alert. His muscles are constantly tense, and he interprets any unexpected delay—a slow elevator, a supplier arriving late—as a sign that something terrible is unfolding just out of his sight. This conviction of imminent danger compels him to engage in constant monitoring. He obsessively checks his body for any unusual sensation, interpreting a slight headache or a moment of breathlessness as a sign the poison is still inside him, reactivating. This core belief that he is broken also makes him exquisitely vulnerable to the traumatic memory; any fleeting feeling of weakness is enough to pull the memory of his collapse back to the forefront of his mind.

The constant feeling of being on alert is exhausting. Feeling his body gripped by such intense fear, often for no discernible reason, has become the most damning evidence for his belief that he is fundamentally broken and can no longer trust his own senses. When his body screams danger for no apparent reason, he tries to regain control by checking his environment, a habit that has become disruptive at work. He finds himself leaving meetings to inspect supply closets or questioning housekeeping staff about cleaning agents. This hypervigilant state acts like a magnet for the trauma, as the feeling of panic itself has become a trigger for the memory to intrude. Each false alarm that sends him checking his pulse or scanning a room reinforces his conviction that he is no longer the capable man he once was, deepening his sense of alienation and his fear that he can no longer trust his own body.

His attempts to manage the distress have only tightened its grip. The compulsive scanning of his surroundings keeps the possibility of another exposure at the forefront of his mind, which in turn makes the intrusive taste and memories more frequent. When colleagues gently try to ask how he is doing, he changes the subject, avoiding any reminder of the event. This avoidance has created a silent distance, preventing him from processing what happened and feeding his painful belief that he no longer belongs, not even among the staff he has managed for years. The very act of checking his body for symptoms often creates the physical sensations he fears; focusing on his breathing makes it feel shallow, which his brain interprets as a new threat, sending a fresh wave of panic through him and validating his terror.

Bao came to therapy after a particularly severe panic attack in the hotel lobby, triggered by the smell of a guest’s metallic perfume. He crumpled onto a bench, gasping for air, convinced he was dying, while his staff and guests looked on. The public nature of his loss of control was the final humiliation. He feels trapped in a cycle of fear he cannot break, and what he wants more than anything is to feel safe in his own skin again, to be able to walk through the halls of his hotel without feeling like he is walking back into that storeroom.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not describe how the patient's sense of threat directly influences or reinforces his negative beliefs.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
